lesson.title: From Gas to Skeleton: What Carbon Fixation Actually Does
lesson.summary: Carbon fixation is the single chemical step where inorganic carbon dioxide gas is attached to an organic molecule for the first time, turning air into the raw material for sugar.
lesson.body:
Almost all the carbon atoms in a plant's sugars, proteins, fats, and structural tissue started out as carbon dioxide molecules drifting in the air. Getting a carbon atom out of that gaseous, inorganic form and into an organic molecule, one built on a carbon backbone with hydrogens attached, is not automatic. Carbon dioxide is a low-energy, stable molecule, and simply mixing it with organic compounds does not make it react. Carbon fixation is the name for the specific enzyme-catalyzed step that overcomes this and forms the first carbon-carbon bond between an incoming CO2 molecule and an already-existing organic carbon skeleton.

In the pathway most plants use, this happens at the very start of the Calvin cycle. A five-carbon sugar called ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, already present in the chloroplast stroma, reacts with an incoming carbon dioxide molecule, and the two combine to form a six-carbon compound. That six-carbon intermediate is extremely unstable and splits apart almost immediately into two molecules of a three-carbon compound. This is why the process is sometimes remembered by simple arithmetic: a five-carbon molecule plus a one-carbon gas gives a six-carbon total, which splits evenly into three plus three.

The three-carbon product of this reaction, 3-phosphoglycerate, is the first stable organic compound the newly fixed carbon appears in, and everything that follows in the Calvin cycle, the reduction of this compound using ATP and NADPH into G3P, and the eventual regeneration of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, depends on this fixation step having happened first. Carbon fixation is therefore the entry point of the whole cycle, the single place where the outside world, in the form of atmospheric gas, connects to the internal chemistry of the plant.

Because this reaction is the doorway through which essentially all new organic carbon enters the biosphere from the atmosphere, the enzyme that catalyzes it operates under enormous demand, fixing a huge quantity of carbon dioxide that plants, algae, and cyanobacteria process globally every day. Not every organism fixes carbon by exactly this route. Some pathways, covered later in this unit, add extra chemical steps before or around this core reaction to cope with hot or dry conditions, but the underlying chemistry, attaching an inorganic carbon dioxide molecule to an organic carbon skeleton, is the same fundamental event in every case.

Understanding carbon fixation as a distinct step, separate from the rest of the Calvin cycle's bookkeeping, matters because it is the point where the entire system is most vulnerable and most heavily regulated. Whatever controls how quickly this first bond forms, whether that is the availability of carbon dioxide, the concentration of the enzyme, or a competing reaction at the same active site, ultimately controls how fast the whole cycle can turn and how much sugar a plant can build.
